title: The Real History of Halloween: Told Through a Small Town's Newspapers

lines.say: Every October, something strange happens on the streets of La Porte, Indiana.
Children dressed as ghosts and witches knock on the doors of strangers and demand candy. And the strangers hand it over.
In 1866, a Philadelphia newspaper described the same night a little differently. Among the night's amusements, it said: hanging dead cats to door-bells.
lines.tts: In eighteen sixty-six, a Philadelphia newspaper described the same night a little differently. Among the night's amusements, it said: hanging dead cats to door-bells.

lines.say: The holiday you know is about a hundred years old. The one underneath it is much, much older. And almost everything you've been told about where it came from is wrong.
lines.lower: Halloween in Scotland | an 1896 engraving for Burns's poem

lines.say: There was no Celtic god of the dead named Samhain. The church did not steal the date. The jack-o'-lantern was a turnip. And trick-or-treat began as a threat.

We'll also tell you what Halloween looked like right here, in La Porte County, over a hundred and fifty years, through the newspapers of the towns around us, and the weather records of the nights themselves.
This is the real history of Halloween: what's documented, what's legend, and what no one can prove.

v.title: THE REAL HISTORY OF HALLOWEEN

lines.say: Start with the part nobody puts on a greeting card. In America, Halloween was a night of vandalism long before it was a night of candy.
In 1872, Godey's Lady's Book, the best-known women's magazine in the country, complained about gangs of boys who, in its words, batter down panels, dislocate bell-wires, and unhinge gates.

lines.say: So here is the question this film is really about. How did a night of broken gates become a night when strangers give your children chocolate?
To answer that, we have to go back about twelve hundred years, to a monastery in Ireland.

card.title: Samhain
card.sub: What the records actually say · Ireland, the 800s

lines.say: You have probably heard that Halloween comes from Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival of the dead, when the veil between the worlds grew thin.
Here is what the records actually say. The word Samhain, the first of November, appears in Irish writing from about the ninth century on.
lines.lower: Stories of Samhain survive in Irish manuscripts copied by monks

lines.say: Those writings were made by Christian monks, copying stories that were already old. In them, Samhain is the start of winter, and the night when kings held their assemblies, and when strange things happen in the tales.

v.head: SAMHAIN IN THE OLD IRISH TALES
rows: The first of November: the start of winter.
Kings hold their assemblies at Tara.
The hero Fionn fights a fire-breathing enemy.
A man named Nera walks among the dead.

lines.say: Archaeologists have dug at the Hill of Ward, in County Meath, where a later legend put the great Samhain fire. They found feasting bones in every layer, and heavy burning, going back about three thousand years.
lines.lower: County Meath, on a 19th-century map of Ireland

lines.say: Was that Samhain? The lead archaeologist's own words were: tempting, but difficult to conclusively prove.

v.cap: Samhain, said to be the source of Halloween

lines.say: No such god appears in any Irish text. He was invented in 1786 by a British army officer named Charles Vallancey, who wrote that the Irish deity Saman was the judge of departed souls. Vallancey, a reviewer said, wrote more nonsense than any man of his time.

lines.say: The Celtic New Year. That one comes from two Victorian scholars, John Rhys and James Frazer, around the turn of the last century. The historian Ronald Hutton checked the medieval records. There is no record of such a festival.
Druids and human sacrifice at Samhain. There is no contemporary record of any pagan Samhain rite at all. Not one.

v.cap: no record of any Samhain rite survives

lines.say: So: a real festival, at the start of winter, with real fires and real stories. A god, a new year, and a sacrifice that were added much later. That's Samhain.
The next thing everyone knows: the church moved All Saints' Day to the first of November to stamp out Samhain. Halloween is just All Hallows' Eve, the night before.

lines.say: The second half is where it gets interesting. Rome's first feast of all the martyrs was in May. In the year 609, Pope Boniface the Fourth dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and the martyrs, on May thirteenth.

lines.say: The November date shows up in England and Germany first. By about the year 800, Charlemagne's favorite churchman, Alcuin, was keeping All Saints on the first of November. In 835, the emperor Louis the Pious made it official across his empire.

lines.say: Now here's the problem for the stamp-out-Samhain theory. We can check what the Irish church itself did. Its calendars show the Irish keeping All Saints on April twentieth. The November date came out of England and the Frankish empire, and Rome adopted it.

v.cap: All Saints' Day in the early Irish church

lines.say: Was it chosen to compete with a pagan festival? Some historians say yes. Hutton says the evidence points the other way. Nobody can prove it either way.

lines.say: The second of November, All Souls' Day, for everyone who had died, was added around the year 1000 by an abbot in France. Now the church had two days for the dead, back to back, at the start of winter.

And that's when the door-knocking starts. In England, from at least 1511, the poor went house to house on All Hallows asking for soul cakes, small spiced cakes, in return for prayers for the family's dead.

lines.say: Burns added footnotes. Young people went out in the dark, hand in hand, eyes shut, and pulled up the first kale stalk they touched. Its shape told them the shape of their future husband or wife.

They named two nuts for a boy and a girl and set them in the fire, to see if they burned together or jumped apart. A girl took a candle, alone, to a mirror, and ate an apple, to see a face appear behind her.

Halloween, in 1785, was a night for finding out who you'd marry. In 1833, the painter Daniel Maclise exhibited a party he'd been to the year before at Blarney, in Ireland, with the same games: bobbing for apples, snapping at an apple on a string.

lines.say: So why did it survive? Because it kept changing. A winter fire became a church feast. A church feast became a night for finding out who you'd marry. That became a night for breaking gates, and that became a deal: treat us, and we'll leave your gate alone.
And every generation told itself the night was ancient, because that made it feel like it belonged to them. Maybe that's the real tradition. Not the turnip, or the pumpkin, or the candy. The story.
